This review discusses the evidence for opportunistic screening for CAC on thoracic CT and highlights novel applications including AI/ML assessments, CAC as a multi-system biomarker, and the potential for photon counting CT.

records.title: Artificial intelligence in hepatopathy diagnosis and treatment: Big data analytics, deep learning, and clinical prediction models.

content.title: Artificial intelligence in hepatopathy diagnosis and treatment: Big data analytics, deep learning, and clinical prediction models.
content.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming the landscape of hepatology by enabling automated data interpretation, early disease detection, and individualized treatment strategies. Chronic liver diseases, including non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma, often progress silently and pose diagnostic challenges due to reliance on invasive biopsies and operator-dependent imaging. This review explores the integration of AI across key domains such as big data analytics, deep learning-based image analysis, histopathological interpretation, biomarker discovery, and clinical prediction modeling. AI algorithms have demonstrated high accuracy in liver fibrosis staging, hepatocellular carcinoma detection, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease risk stratification, while also enhancing survival prediction and treatment response assessment. For instance, convolutional neural networks trained on portal venous-phase computed tomography have achieved area under the curves up to 0.92 for significant fibrosis (F2-F4) and 0.89 for advanced fibrosis, with magnetic resonance imaging-based models reporting comparable performance. Advanced methodologies such as federated learning preserve patient privacy during cross-center model training, and explainable AI techniques promote transparency and clinician trust. Despite these advancements, clinical adoption remains limited by challenges including data heterogeneity, algorithmic bias, regulatory uncertainty, and lack of real-time integration into electronic health records. Looking forward, the convergence of multi-omics, imaging, and clinical data through interpretable and validated AI frameworks holds great promise for precision liver care. Continued efforts in model standardization, ethical oversight, and clinician-centered deployment will be essential to realize the full potential of AI in hepatopathy diagnosis and treatment.

records.title: Getting your publication right - Part 4 structuring a research manuscript: A guide to understanding, detecting, and preventing plagiarism.
records.publisher: Journal of conservative dentistry and endodontics

content.title: Getting your publication right - Part 4 structuring a research manuscript: A guide to understanding, detecting, and preventing plagiarism.
content.abstract: Plagiarism is one of the most persistent ethical problems in academic and scientific publishing. Once limited to copying sentences from books, it has grown into a far more complicated challenge, driven by the internet, intense research competition, and the rapid spread of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools. This article provides a thorough overview of plagiarism - definition, historical roots, types, contributing factors, detection tools, and regulatory frameworks with particular focus on recent developments through 2025/2026. The article pays special attention to India's regulatory approach under the University Grants Commission 2018 Regulations, the global role of the Committee on Publication Ethics, and the newly published Generative AI Transparency 2024 guidelines. The central argument is that addressing plagiarism today demands a combination of good ethical education, clear institutional policies, honest AI disclosure, and a genuine commitment to original thinking.

records.title: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of integrated traditional Chinese and conventional medicine for ulcerative colitis.

content.title: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of integrated traditional Chinese and conventional medicine for ulcerative colitis.
content.abstract:
Objective

To optimize clinical management of ulcerative colitis (UC) and evaluate the efficacy of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), conventional medicine (CM), and integrated TCM- CM therapies.

Methods

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) investigating integrated TCM-CM treatment for UC were retrieved from PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang Data, VIP Database, and SinoMed from database inception to June 2025. Study quality was assessed using Review Manager 5.4 and the 7-point Jadad scale. Statistical analyses were performed using Stata MP 15 and R 4.3.1 with Rstudio.

Results

A total of 46 RCTs involving 3,763 patients with UC were included, comprising seven intervention regimens: four commercial Chinese polyherbal preparation (e.g., Yunnan Baiyao) and sixteen classical TCM decoctions (TCMDs; e.g., Baitouweng Decoction). The results showed that conventional medicine combined with TCMD and acupoint catgut embedding achieved the highest total effective rate. CM alone ranked highest in alleviating key clinical symptoms (e.g., diarrhea and abdominal pain) and in reducing inflammatory markers, including IL-8, C-reactive protein (CRP), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). For cytokine regulation, comparative advantages varied across interventions: CM + TCMD + acupuncture ranked highest for IL-6 reduction, CM + TCMD ranked highest for IL-10 improvement, whereas CM alone ranked lower for these two outcomes.

Conclusion

Compared with the single use of conventinal medicine, the combined use of traditional Chinese and conventinal medicine in the treatment of ulcerative colitis demonstrates greater overall efficacy. Through network meta-analysis, this study identified optimal intervention regimens for different outcome indicators, including both monotherapy and combination therapy. In clinical practice, the optimal regimens may be selected according to individual patient conditions. Although TCM interventions can improve clinical symptoms and inflammatory biomarkers in patients with ulcerative colitis, relevant clinical score improvement and endoscopic mucosal healing evidence are still insufficient. Further high-quality clinical evidence is still required to confirm the definite clinical efficacy of TCM.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/display_record.php?RecordID=1109183, identifier CRD420251109183.

records.title: The use of MRI in the diagnosis of ovarian cancer.

content.title: The use of MRI in the diagnosis of ovarian cancer.
content.abstract: Ovarian cancer is a malignant tumor of the female reproductive system with a high mortality rate. Currently, China has the highest number of new ovarian cancer cases worldwide; therefore, preoperative diagnosis is of particular importance. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), with its excellent soft tissue resolution and absence of ionizing radiation risk, has become a key imaging modality for the non-invasive diagnosis of ovarian cancer in clinical practice. This article systematically reviews the latest research advances in the application of conventional morphological MRI, multiparametric MRI, and the integration of MRI with radiomics and deep learning technologies in the diagnosis and treatment of ovarian cancer. It focuses on their clinical value in assessing the benign or malignant nature of ovarian tumors, classifying pathological subtypes of epithelial and non-epithelial ovarian cancers, staging ovarian cancer, monitoring treatment efficacy, and predicting prognosis. Additionally, it outlines research directions for emerging technologies such as molecular probes. Existing studies have confirmed that multimodal MRI fusion technology can significantly improve the diagnostic accuracy of ovarian cancer; however, challenges remain, including a lack of model generalizability, insufficient interpretability, difficulty in detecting micro-lesions, and low clinical adoption rates. Future efforts should focus on establishing standardized MRI scanning protocols and data standards, conducting large-scale, multicenter prospective studies, deepening the integrated application of interpretable artificial intelligence and molecular imaging, and constructing an integrated "imaging-biology-clinical" precision assessment system to advance the development of precision preoperative diagnosis and treatment for ovarian cancer.

records.title: Prognostic value of AI-enabled quantitative coronary CT angiography for major adverse cardiovascular events: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
records.publisher: International journal of cardiology. Cardiovascular risk and prevention

content.title: Prognostic value of AI-enabled quantitative coronary CT angiography for major adverse cardiovascular events: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Artificial intelligence-enabled quantitative coronary computed tomography angiography (AI-QCCTA) offers automated assessment of coronary plaque burden and morphology. Although AI-QCCTA has improved diagnostic consistency and downstream testing efficiency, its prognostic value for major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) has not been comprehensively quantified.

Methods

We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane through October 2025 for studies evaluating AI-based plaque analysis in patients without prior MACE undergoing CCTA. Outcomes of interest were pooled using random-effects GLMM models, and prognostic associations were synthesized using inverse-variance random-effects meta-analysis of hazard ratios (HRs). The primary endpoint was MACE; secondary outcomes included myocardial infarction (MI), revascularization, angina, stroke, and mortality. Subgroup analysis was done to identify the association of different plaque characteristics in predicting MACE/MI/Death.

Results

Ten studies (n = 20,195) were included. Across six cohorts (n = 18,804), pooled rates were: all-cause mortality 1.20% (95% CI 0.38-3.77%), cardiovascular mortality 0.32% (0.21-0.48%), MACE 5.07% (1.25-18.46%), MI 1.30% (0.41-3.99%), and revascularization 13.09% (6.57-24.40%). AI-enabled plaque burden predicted MACE (HR 1.95, 95% CI 1.29-2.94; I2 = 99%), consistent in sensitivity analysis as per same AI platform use (HR 1.88, 95% CI 1.15-3.07). Low-attenuation plaque showed the strongest association (HR 2.95, 95% CI 1.95-4.45).

Conclusions

AI-QCCTA provides prognostic value beyond stenosis severity, with vulnerable plaque characteristics-particularly low-attenuation and non-calcified plaque most strongly predicting adverse cardiovascular outcomes. These findings support the integration of AI-enabled plaque analysis into contemporary risk stratification.

records.title: Age- and region-specific gut microbiota dysbiosis in axial spondyloarthritis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Age- and region-specific gut microbiota dysbiosis in axial spondyloarthritis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) is a chronic inflammatory disease affecting the spine and sacroiliac joints. Emerging evidence suggests that the gut microbiota may contribute to its pathogenesis, but findings on microbial diversity and composition remain inconsistent.

Methods

We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library to identify studies comparing the gut microbiota between adults with axSpA and healthy controls. α-Diversity (Observed richness, Shannon, Simpson, Chao1, ACE) and microbial composition at the phylum level were extracted. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed using standardized mean differences (SMDs), with subgroup analyses and robustness checks (prespecified sensitivity and leave-one-out analyses).

Results

Twenty-five studies (n = 1639) were included. Compared with controls, axSpA was associated with lower α-diversity for Observed richness (SMD = -0.59, P = 0.04), Shannon (SMD = -0.19, P = 0.03), and Chao1 (SMD = -0.51, P = 0.02), while Simpson (SMD = -0.23, P = 0.12) and ACE (SMD = 0.42, P = 0.14) showed no significant differences. In age-stratified analyses, reductions were more apparent in participants >40 years (Shannon: SMD = -0.38, P = 0.002; Simpson: SMD = -0.50, P = 0.001). Sensitivity and leave-one-out analyses were directionally consistent; however, observed richness and Shannon became non-significant after excluding non-comparable datasets. Phylum-level findings were summarized descriptively, suggesting lower Bacteroidota and Actinobacteriota and higher Proteobacteria in axSpA.

Conclusion

axSpA is associated with reduced α-diversity and compositional shifts in gut microbiota, but the magnitude of effects varies across studies. Heterogeneity and methodological differences warrant cautious interpretation. Longitudinal and functional studies are needed to clarify causality and therapeutic implications.

records.title: Seafarer fatigue: a systematic review and narrative synthesis of concepts, risk factors, prediction methods, and risk management strategies.

content.title: Seafarer fatigue: a systematic review and narrative synthesis of concepts, risk factors, prediction methods, and risk management strategies.
content.abstract: Seafarer fatigue is a major contributing factor to maritime accidents and has gained widespread attention in the shipping industry. However, existing evidence remains fragmented across different fatigue concepts, measurement approaches, risk factors, prediction models, and management strategies. This systematic review and narrative synthesis aimed to critically synthesize current evidence on seafarer fatigue, with particular attention to its conceptualization, risk factors, subgroup differences, prediction approaches, and fatigue risk management strategies. A systematic search was conducted in Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, CNKI, and Wanfang from January 2000 to April 2026. Additional studies were identified through citation searching. After screening and eligibility assessment, 56 studies were included. Owing to substantial heterogeneity in study designs, populations, fatigue definitions, measurement tools, and outcomes, no meta-analysis was conducted; instead, findings were synthesized narratively. The review indicates that seafarer fatigue is a multidimensional phenomenon shaped by sleep and recovery conditions, work organization, shipboard environmental stressors, individual and psychosocial factors, and organizational or regulatory contexts. This review highlights the need for clearer fatigue concepts, stronger subgroup-specific evidence, externally validated prediction models, and integrated fatigue risk management systems tailored to diverse maritime working conditions.

records.title: Artificial intelligence in surgical decision-making across the perioperative continuum: a scoping review.

content.title: Artificial intelligence in surgical decision-making across the perioperative continuum: a scoping review.
content.abstract:
Background

The role of artificial intelligence (AI) in supporting clinical decision-making across the perioperative continuum remains incompletely defined. Although the presence of many AI models that perform well in terms of their predictive performance has been established, their role in the actual surgical decision-making process in the real-world in terms of specialties and perioperative phases has not been fully mapped.

Objective

To map the existing literature on the application of AI in surgical decision-making across the perioperative continuum, describe its use in preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative phases, and identify key barriers and gaps affecting clinical implementation.

Methods

A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched for studies evaluating AI applications in surgical decision-making. Eligible studies included primary research and evidence syntheses applying machine learning, deep learning, radiomics, or computer vision to diagnosis, risk stratification, surgical planning, intraoperative guidance, or postoperative outcome prediction. Study characteristics, perioperative phase, clinical application, AI methodology, and reported implementation barriers were extracted and charted using a standardized data form.

Results

Fifty- five sources of evidence were included. Sources addressing multiple or cross-phase perioperative applications constituted the largest category, while among phase-specific applications, preoperative applications were the most frequent and primarily focused on diagnosis, risk stratification, and surgical planning. Intraoperative applications were less common and were limited by data availability, workflow integration, and real-time implementation challenges. Postoperative applications mainly addressed complication prediction, survival estimation, and recovery monitoring.

Conclusion

AI in surgical decision-making is expanding rapidly, with preoperative applications showing comparatively greater evidence maturity than intraoperative and postoperative applications. However, prospective validation and real-world implementation remain limited across the perioperative continuum.

records.title: Radiomics for Detection and Differentiation of Intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

content.title: Radiomics for Detection and Differentiation of Intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (ICC) is an aggressive primary liver malignancy with limited survival, largely due to delayed diagnosis, recurrence and limited effective therapeutic options. Radiomics- and artificial intelligence (AI)-based imaging models have emerged as promising tools to improve noninvasive detection and differentiation of ICC. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the diagnostic performance of radiomics-based AI models for ICC.

Methods

A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library was performed from inception through 2025 in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Studies assessing radiomics- or AI-based models derived from CT, MRI, PET, or ultrasound for differentiation of ICC from other hepatic lesions were included. Pooled sensitivity, specificity, positive likelihood ratio (PLR), and negative likelihood ratio (NLR) were estimated using a bivariate random-effects model. Study quality and risk of bias were assessed using the Radiomics Quality Score (RQS) and QUADAS-2 tools.

Results

Twenty retrospective studies comprising 8746 participants were included. Across pooled validation and test datasets, radiomics-based AI models demonstrated a pooled sensitivity of 0.77 (95% CI, 0.69-0.84) and specificity of 0.88 (95% CI, 0.78-0.94) for differentiating ICC from non-ICC hepatic lesions. The pooled PLR was 6.81 (95% CI, 3.51-13.2), and the pooled NLR was 0.23 (95% CI, 0.09-0.61). CT-based models showed higher diagnostic performance compared with MRI and ultrasound. Subgroup and meta-regression analyses identified imaging modality, contrast phase, segmentation strategy, and validation approach as contributors to interstudy heterogeneity. The overall methodological quality demonstrated a mean Radiomics Quality Score (RQS) of 14.0 (range 11-24), corresponding to approximately 39% of the maximum achievable score. External validation cohorts were incorporated in 60% of the studies, although adherence to standardized feature reproducibility frameworks varied.

Conclusions

Radiomics-based AI models demonstrate clinically meaningful diagnostic accuracy for noninvasive differentiation of ICC and may complement conventional imaging in preoperative evaluation. Prospective, multicenter studies with standardized imaging protocols and rigorous external validation are required before routine clinical adoption.

records.title: Role of artificial intelligence in gastric diseases.

content.title: Role of artificial intelligence in gastric diseases.
content.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in gastroenterology has evolved from basic computer-aided detection to sophisticated multimodal frameworks that enable real-time clinical decision support. This study presents AI applications in gastric disease diagnosis and management, highlighting the transition from domain-specific deep learning to general-purpose large language models. Our research reveals a key finding: AI effectiveness demonstrates an inverse relationship with user expertise, with moderate-expertise practitioners benefiting the most, whereas experts and novices show limited performance gains. We developed a clinical decision support system achieving 96% lesion detection internally and 82%-87% classification accuracy in external validation. Multimodal integration, which combines endoscopic images, clinical histories, laboratory results, and genomic data, enables comprehensive disease assessment and personalized treatment. The emergence of large language models with expanding context windows and multiagent architectures represents a paradigm shift in medical AI. Furthermore, emerging technologies are expanding AI's potential applications, and feasibility studies on smart glasses in endoscopy training suggest opportunities for hands-free assistance, although clinical implementation challenges persist. This minireview addresses persistent limitations including geographic bias in training data, regulatory hurdles, ethical considerations regarding patient privacy and AI accountability, and the concentration of AI development among technology giants. Successful integration requires balancing innovation with patient safety, while preserving the irreplaceable role of human clinical judgment.

records.title: Is plant-based protein supplementation as effective as whey protein? A systematic review and meta-analysis in untrained adults undergoing resistance training.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Is plant-based protein supplementation as effective as whey protein? A systematic review and meta-analysis in untrained adults undergoing resistance training.
content.abstract:
Background

Dietary protein supplements are commonly consumed to support increases in lean body mass among healthy adults engaged in resistance training (RT). Although whey protein has been extensively investigated, plant-based protein supplements have emerged as a viable alternative for individuals who avoid animal-derived products.

Methods

The present study aims to evaluate, through a systematic review and meta-analysis, the effects of plant-based versus whey protein supplementation on body composition in untrained adults (18-59 years) undergoing RT, using Dual-Energy X-Ray Absorptiometry (DEXA). The systematic review was conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 checklist and was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251145410). Searches were conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect, identifying 5 studies that met the inclusion criteria for qualitative synthesis and meta-analysis.

Results

When combined with RT, both plant-based and whey protein supplementation were associated with improvements in lean body mass (LBM) and body fat mass (BFM), with no significant between-group differences observed.

Conclusions

Thus, soy- and pea-based protein supplements may support favorable body composition changes in adults initiating RT and could be considered practical nutritional options for individuals seeking alternatives to whey protein. Regarding chia-based protein, the available evidence is currently limited to a single study that did not demonstrate significant changes in lean body mass; therefore, firm conclusions regarding its efficacy cannot be drawn at this time.

records.title: Lower-Body Strength and Hypertrophy Adaptations in Response to Concurrent Training in Trained Young Males.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Lower-Body Strength and Hypertrophy Adaptations in Response to Concurrent Training in Trained Young Males.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Gomes, M, Costa, M, Pezarat-Correia, P, and Mendonca, GV. Lower-body strength and hypertrophy adaptations in response to concurrent training in trained young males. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study examined the interference effect of concurrent training (CT) on maximal and explosive strength and muscle morphology in trained young males. Thirty subjects were randomly assigned to endurance training (E), resistance training (R), or CT for 11 weeks. The intervention comprised 2 mesocycles: weeks 1-5 emphasizing maximal strength, and weeks 6-11 targeting explosive strength. Assessments were conducted at baseline, mid-training, and post-training, and included leg-press maximal voluntary isometric contraction (MVIC), rate of force development (RFD), countermovement jump kinetics, and vastus lateralis cross-sectional area and pennation angle. Maximal voluntary isometric contraction increased only in the R group (18.4 ± 10.2%, p = 0.015). Peak RFD improved in both R (31.8 ± 23.2%) and CT (23.1 ± 27.9%), although with distinct time courses: R improved progressively across both mesocycles, whereas CT improved only during the second. Early-phase RFD (0-50 ms) increased in the R group from mid-training onward, whereas the CT group improved only from mid- to post-training (38.3 ± 40.4%, p = 0.021), accompanied by greater quadriceps electromyographic activity (p < 0.05). No changes in RFD were observed in E during training. Countermovement jump positive impulse improved in both R (12.7 ± 9.0%) and CT (8.8 ± 8.3%, p < 0.05), with no evidence of interference in jump-related explosive performance. Cross-sectional area increased in both R (17.0 ± 13.0%) and CT (8.8 ± 9.4%, p < 0.05). Pennation angle increased in CT (10.1 ± 12.9%) and R (18.6 ± 15.1%). These findings indicate that, although CT may limit MVIC development and delay early-phase RFD adaptations, it does not hinder explosive performance when resistance training is oriented toward rapid-strength development. Thus, CT can be effectively implemented in trained individuals when resistance training is periodized to emphasize neural-driven explosive or hypertrophy-related adaptations.

records.title: Effects of Resistance Training on Isometric Force and Muscle Thickness in Prepubertal and Pubertal Boys: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Effects of Resistance Training on Isometric Force and Muscle Thickness in Prepubertal and Pubertal Boys: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Komm, YN, Held, S, Gavanda, S, Comfort, P, Faigenbaum, AD, Geisler, S, and Augste, C. Effects of resistance training on isometric force and muscle thickness in prepubertal and pubertal boys: a randomized controlled trial. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-While increases in strength in youth are largely attributed to neural adaptations, evidence regarding hypertrophic adaptations in prepubertal youth remains inconsistent. This study compared the effects of resistance training on hypertrophy and strength between prepubertal and pubertal adolescents. Sixty-eight male subjects were classified as prepubertal (11.58 ± 1.04 years) or pubertal (14.28 ± 0.88 years) using maturity offset estimates and randomized into 4 groups: prepubertal resistance training (n = 19), prepubertal active control (n = 20), pubertal resistance training (n = 14), and pubertal active control (n = 15). The 9-week intervention consisted of 2 weekly sessions of lower-body resistance training, while the active control groups continued their regular soccer training. Strength was assessed using the isometric mid-thigh pull, and hypertrophy was assessed using muscle thickness. Data were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. No significant Time × Intervention interactions were observed for rectus femoris and vastus intermedius (p = 0.295), and for vastus lateralis (p = 0.711). A significant Time × Intervention interaction (p = 0.042) was found for peak force, indicating superior strength improvements in the training groups. No significant Time × Maturity × Intervention interactions were detected for absolute strength (p = 0.289), relative strength (p = 0.656), rectus femoris and vastus intermedius thickness (p = 0.451), or vastus lateralis thickness (p = 0.731), although these analyses had limited statistical power. These findings indicate that the resistance training protocol in this study increased isometric mid-thigh pull force in prepubertal and pubertal adolescent boys.

records.title: Regional lean mass, bone mineral measures, and estimated leg press 1-RM in resistance-trained males.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Regional lean mass, bone mineral measures, and estimated leg press 1-RM in resistance-trained males.
content.abstract:
Background

Regional lean mass, bone mineral content (BMC), and strength are related in young men, but it is less clear how much these relationships simply reflect shared body and skeletal size in resistance-trained individuals. We therefore examined broad regional associations between lean mass and bone measures, together with selected bone and function relationships, with particular attention to body size.

Methods

This cross-sectional secondary analysis used baseline data from 44 resistance-trained males from a previous four group trial. Whole body dual energy X ray absorptiometry (DXA) provided broad upper body and lower body lean mass measures, BMC, projected bone area, and areal bone mineral density (BMD). We examined associations using Pearson correlations and linear regression with HC3 robust standard errors. Models adjusted for age and height were considered alongside body mass, projected area, and allometric models. Benjamini Hochberg correction across all 18 adjusted cross-sectional tests was prioritized.

Results

Regional lean mass was positively associated with several BMC outcomes in models adjusted for age and height, including arm BMC (standardized β = 0.605), rib BMC (β = 0.608), leg BMC (β = 0.429), and pelvis BMC (β = 0.550). Several estimates became smaller or less precise when body mass, projected bone area, or allometric scaling was considered. Pelvis BMC was conditionally associated with estimated leg press 1-RM after adjustment for age, height, and lower body lean mass (β = 0.501; 18 test BH q = 0.001). This association, however, cannot distinguish the influence of skeletal size, body proportions, training history, or other unmeasured factors.

Conclusions

In resistance-trained males, regional DXA lean mass and bone measures appear to form a phenotype that is strongly influenced by body size. Associations from models adjusted for age and height should therefore be interpreted alongside the size conditioned analyzes. The association between pelvis BMC and estimated leg press 1-RM is best viewed as an exploratory conditional finding within this broader phenotype, rather than evidence of a distinct skeletal contribution to strength.

records.title: Effects of In-Season Contrast Strength Training on Jump Performance and Sprint Ability in Female Field Hockey Players.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Effects of In-Season Contrast Strength Training on Jump Performance and Sprint Ability in Female Field Hockey Players.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Chilingirian-Padrón, R, Álvarez-Yates, T, and García-García, O. Effects of in-season contrast strength training on jump performance and sprint ability in female field hockey players. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The purpose of this study was to examine the effects of a 6-week in-season contrast strength training program incorporating sport-specific tasks on neuromuscular performance in sub-elite female field hockey players. Twenty-five athletes completed a pre-post single-cohort intervention integrated into their regular team schedule. Each session consisted of 3 sequential blocks: (a) a high-load strength exercise targeting maximal strength or hypertrophy (70-85% 1 repetition maximum [1RM]); (b) a biomechanically related explosive action performed at low load (∼30% 1RM) and high execution velocity; and (c) a high-speed sport-specific task. Jump performance was assessed using bilateral and unilateral countermovement jumps (CMJs) and free arm CMJ, whereas sprint ability was evaluated through 10- and 20-m sprints. A mixed-model repeated-measures analysis of variance was used to determine the effects of the intervention, with Time (Pre, Post) as within-subject factor and Playing Position (defenders, midfielders, forwards) as between-subject factor, with the level of significance set at p ≤ 0.05. Significant improvements were observed in all jump and sprint assessments: jump performance increased by 5.7-29.6%, whereas sprint ability improved by 1.6-1.9%. These findings indicate that 6 weeks of contrast strength training incorporating high-speed sports-specific tasks performed during the competitive season elicited meaningful improvements in stretch-shortening cycle-related jump performance and sprint ability in sub-elite female field hockey players.

records.title: Comparison of Functional and Traditional Strength and Power Training on U19 Soccer Players During Offseason in Norway: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Comparison of Functional and Traditional Strength and Power Training on U19 Soccer Players During Offseason in Norway: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Engberg Treu Lassen, L, Kersting, UG, and Pessoto Hirata, R. Comparison of functional and traditional strength and power training on U19 soccer players during off-season in Norway: A randomized controlled trial. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Functional training emphasizes multiplanar, soccer-specific movement patterns requiring body control, whereas traditional resistance training focuses on maximal force production through stable, bilateral lifts. Although both approaches are common in soccer physical preparation, their relative effects on soccer-specific performance remain uncertain. This study compared the effects of functional vs. traditional strength training on performance outcomes during the offseason in U19 male players. Thirty-three Norwegian players were randomly allocated to a functional training group (FTG, n = 11), a traditional training group (TTG, n = 11), or a control group (CG, n = 11) using stratified, concealed allocation. During the first 4 weeks, all groups completed 2 weekly soccer sessions; FTG and TTG additionally completed 2 supervised 70-minute strength sessions per week. In the final 4 weeks, FTG and TTG continued the twice-weekly strength training, whereas CG ceased organized training. Functional training group performed unilateral, multiplanar free-weight exercises, while TTG performed bilateral, uniplanar machine-based exercises. The primary outcome was technical soccer performance, with mobility, dynamic balance, sprint speed, change of direction, and vertical jump as secondary outcomes. Both FTG and TTG improved Loughborough Soccer Shooting Test (LSST) performance compared with CG (FTG: -0.43 seconds, p = 0.003, d = 1.62; TTG: -0.50 seconds, p < 0.001, d = 1.88). Traditional training group also increased body mass compared with the CG (2.20 kg, p = 0.002, d = 1.65). Functional and traditional strength training produced comparable improvements in LSST time. These findings highlight training dose response and support individualized off-season programs integrating physical preparation with sport-specific demands.

records.title: Acute Molecular and Chronic Vastus Lateralis Adaptations to Lengthened Partial versus Full Range of Motion Resistance Training in Trained Men.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Acute Molecular and Chronic Vastus Lateralis Adaptations to Lengthened Partial versus Full Range of Motion Resistance Training in Trained Men.
content.abstract:
Purpose

This study examined how lower-body lengthened partial (LP) versus full range of motion (FULL) resistance training affects acute post-exercise signaling, chronic hypertrophy, and cellular adaptations of the vastus lateralis (VL) muscle in resistance-trained men.

Methods

Eight males (22±1 years old, 5.6±1.4 years training) completed a crossover study whereby VL biopsies were collected pre-exercise and 0, 3, and 24 hours following LP and FULL leg extension bouts for transcriptomic and anabolic signaling analyses (Experiment 1). Another 16 males (26±5 years old; 8.0±4.9 years training) completed an 8-week, twice-weekly lower-body intervention using a within-subject design (Experiment 2). One leg was assigned to FULL and the contralateral leg to LP training across three exercises (leg press, leg extension, and lying leg curl). Pre- and post-intervention outcomes included VL muscle cross-sectional area (mCSA) summed across five MRI-derived slices and mid-thigh VL biopsy outcomes.

Results

In Experiment 1, time-dependent changes in the VL transcriptome and anabolic (mTORC1 and Hippo) signaling occurred, but minimal between-protocol interactions existed. In Experiment 2, VL mCSA increased over time (mean change: 9.3cm², 95% CI [6.8, 11.8], P<0.001), with no evidence of differential change between protocols (LP-FULL change: -1.4cm², 95% CI [-6.1, 3.8], P=0.640). Additionally, no significant interactions existed for type I or II fiber CSA (P=0.476, P=0.350), type I or II fiber myonuclei (P=0.813, P=0.589), type I or II satellite cell number (P=0.102, P=0.797), or total RNA content (P=0.537).

Conclusions

This exploratory study suggests that 8 weeks of LP and FULL resistance training elicit similar acute and chronic VL responses in previously trained men.

records.title: Impact of different protein sources on acute muscle protein synthesis following resistance training: a systematic review with standard and dose-response network meta-analyses.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Impact of different protein sources on acute muscle protein synthesis following resistance training: a systematic review with standard and dose-response network meta-analyses.
content.abstract:
Background

The combination of protein intake and resistance training (RT) plays a pivotal role in stimulating muscle protein synthesis (MPS), yet the impact of different protein sources remains an area of active investigation. Therefore, a systematic review incorporating standard and dose‒response network meta-analyses was performed.

Methods

Systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, EBSCOhost (including MEDLINE, SPORTDiscus, CINAHL), and Scopus. Eligible studies included healthy adults (≥18 years) who were undergoing acute resistance exercise followed by a single protein bolus (any type or dose, except blends or enriched with anabolic agents). Muscle biopsies were required before and after RT/protein intake without additional food in between. Trials measuring hourly MPS rates via tracer techniques were included (n = 51).

Results

In the standard network meta-analysis (NMA), native whey (P-score = 0.81, MD = 0.05% [0.00; 0.10]), pea protein (0.77, MD = 0.05% [-0.02; 0.11]), whole egg protein (0.72, MD = 0.04% [-0.01; 0.09]), mycoprotein (0.66, MD = 0.03% [-0.02; 0.08]), and whey protein (0.58, MD = 0.02% [0.01; 0.04]) ranked highest for estimated efficacy in stimulating post-RT hourly MPS (in descending order) (only whey protein showed a statistically significant effect) with low to moderate certainty of evidence. Dose‒response NMA revealed that certain animal- (native whey and whole egg protein) and plant- (pea and mycoprotein) based protein sources to show the highest predicted MPS responses with doses of 18-25 g.

Conclusions

Animal- (native whey, whey, whole egg) and plant-based (pea, mycoprotein) proteins ranked similarly for estimated acute MPS stimulation when combined with RT; however, only whey protein showed a statistically significant effect, and protein sources represented by few studies should be interpreted with caution.

records.title: Effect of tangeretin supplements on simulated precompetition weight loss in female combat sports athletes.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Effect of tangeretin supplements on simulated precompetition weight loss in female combat sports athletes.
content.abstract:
Background

Weight reduction before competition has long been a major challenge for combat-sports athletes. Unscientific weight-loss practices not only increase the risk of hormonal imbalance, electrolyte disturbance, and impaired immune function but also compromise athletic capacities such as aerobic and anaerobic performance and explosive power. This study investigated the potential benefits of tangeretin, a natural citrus extract, on athletic performance. These benefits include the regulation of hormone secretion, the optimization of carbohydrate and lipid metabolism, and the promotion of muscle synthesis and lipid utilization, which may help athletes reach their target weight.

Objective

To examine the effects of tangeretin supplementation on body-composition and sports-performance indicators in female combat-sports athletes, and to evaluate its efficacy for simulated precompetition weight loss.

Methods

Thirty female combat-sports athletes (4 wrestlers, 3 boxers, 9 sanda athletes, 3 judokas, and 11 taekwondo athletes) were recruited. A paired, randomized, double-blind design was used. All 30 participants were first paired according to sport and competitive level, then randomly allocated to either a tangeretin group or a placebo group (15 per group). The 30-day intervention comprised a double-blind nutritional supplement, a dietary questionnaire, blood sampling and analysis, body-composition assessment, isokinetic muscle-strength testing, and aerobic-capacity testing, to evaluate the effects of tangeretin (400 mg/day) on performance and health-related outcomes. These outcomes included body-composition indicators (e.g. body-fat percentage, fat mass, lean-body mass), fat-distribution indicators (e.g. limb and regional fat mass, gynoid fat mass), glucose and lipid-metabolism indicators (e.g. LDL-C, total cholesterol, free fatty acids), hormone indicators (e.g. cortisol, testosterone), muscle-strength indicators (e.g. peak torque of hip, knee, and ankle flexors and extensors), and maximal-oxygen-uptake-derived indicators (e.g. VO2max heart rate, time to exhaustion). Statistical significance was assessed using two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA).

Results

(1) Body weight: 80.0% of athletes in the tangeretin group lost weight to varying degrees, and 33.3% (5 athletes) reached their competition weight class. (2) Body fat: body-fat percentage in the tangeretin group decreased from 23.92 ± 0.87% to 22.92 ± 0.89%; trunk, upper-limb, lower-limb, and android-region fat mass decreased by 6.77%, 8.77%, 4.43%, and 8.09%, respectively. (3) Glucose and lipid metabolism: HDL-C increased by 8.86% (P = 0.002), whereas triglycerides decreased by 25.00% (P = 0.048). (4) Sports performance: peak torque during hip, knee, and ankle flexion and extension increased significantly in the tangeretin group. VO2max also improved from 42.80 ± 1.13 to 43.46 ± 1.32 ml/kg/min.

Conclusion

Tangeretin supplementation effectively reduced body weight and fat mass (both overall and regionally) in female combat-sports athletes. Among the participants, 80.0% lost weight to varying degrees, and 33.3% reached their competition weight class, indicating a strong effect on precompetition weight loss. Moreover, tangeretin improved aerobic capacity and lower-limb joint muscle strength, thereby enhancing competitive performance.

records.title: Effects of Prolonged Combined Aerobic and Strength Training on Movement Velocities During a Strength Loading Bout: Targeting Same Versus Separate Muscle Groups.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Effects of Prolonged Combined Aerobic and Strength Training on Movement Velocities During a Strength Loading Bout: Targeting Same Versus Separate Muscle Groups.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Feuerbacher, JF, Jacobs, MW, Dragutinovic, B, Rehbein, P, and Schumann, M. Effects of prolonged combined aerobic and strength training on movement velocities during a strength loading bout: targeting same versus separate muscle groups. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Combined aerobic and strength training may impair explosive strength performance, especially when targeting the same muscle groups. This study aimed to assess the effects of prolonged combined aerobic and strength training on movement velocities and velocity loss during a strength loading bout when the aerobic and strength training target the same vs. separate muscle groups. Thirty-two men participated in a 12-week intervention, divided into 3 groups: (a) LHLS (lower-body high-intensity interval training (HIIT) and strength training), (b) LHUS (lower-body HIIT and upper-body strength training), and (c) LSUS (lower- and upper-body strength training). Changes in the area under the mean propulsive velocity (MPV) and velocity-loss curves during strength loadings were analyzed pre- and postintervention. Squat performance was compared between LHLS and LSUS, while bench press performance was compared between LHUS and LSUS. The level of significance was set at ρ ≤ 0.05. During bench press loading, no statistically significant main effects for group ( p = 0.225), for timepoint ( p = 0.170), nor group × timepoint ( p = 0.943) were observed for MPV. In squat loading, a statistically significant main effect for timepoint was found ( p = 0.020), with a decrease in MPV for LHLS postintervention ( p = 0.006). The interaction between group and timepoint was not statistically significant ( p = 0.083). No statistically significant main effects for group ( p = 0.110, p = 0.076), for timepoint ( p = 0.590, p = 0.244), nor group × timepoint ( p = 0.626, p = 0.239) were observed for velocity loss in either bench press or squat loading. These findings suggest that explosive strength performance may be more susceptible to interference when aerobic and strength training target the same, rather than different, muscle groups.

records.title: Performance and Physiological Responses to Strength Training Programs in Elite Judo Athletes.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Performance and Physiological Responses to Strength Training Programs in Elite Judo Athletes.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Campos, BT, Rodrigues, JGdS, Cal Abad, CC, Bachi, ALL, dos Santos, CMM, Tritto, AC, Kons, RL, Penna, EM, and Prado, LS. Performance and physiological responses to strength training programs in elite judo athletes. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study compared the effects of 2 short-term strength training models, block planning (BP) and undulating planning (UP), on performance, physiological, and perceptual responses in elite judo athletes. We hypothesized that BP would induce greater physiological strain due to the concentration of training stimuli. Eighteen judokas (14 men and 4 women) were randomly assigned to BP (n = 9) or UP (n = 9) for 4 weeks, performing 6 weekly strength sessions alongside technical-tactical training. Performance outcomes included countermovement jump (CMJ), muscle power (back squat and bent-over row), and the Special Judo Fitness Test (SJFT). Monitoring variables included internal load, heart rate variability (HRV), and well-being, while physiological markers included creatine kinase, tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and cortisol. Data were analyzed using 2-way repeated-measures ANOVA (p < 0.05). Both groups improved SJFT performance (p < 0.01), with no between-group differences. Block planning increased lower-limb peak power (p = 0.01; d = 0.90), whereas UP showed no meaningful change. Upper-limb power and CMJ did not change in either group. Internal load showed different temporal patterns between models. Block planning presented higher HRVcv values (p = 0.04), indicating greater autonomic perturbation. Creatine kinase and TNF-α increased over time in both groups (p ≤ 0.05), while cortisol showed an interaction without clear post hoc differences. In conclusion, BP improved lower-limb power but increased physiological strain, whereas UP elicited similar judo-specific improvements with lower recovery demands. These findings highlight the importance of training organization for balancing performance and recovery in elite judo athletes.

records.title: International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: diets for body weight reduction.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: diets for body weight reduction.
content.abstract: The International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN) has developed an official position on diets for body weight reduction. This critical analysis of the literature is intended to provide a scientific foundation for practitioners, coaches, and trainees regarding the effects of the major diet types in adults who are generally healthy, physically active, and/or athletic, while drawing from clinical research in those with overweight/obesity, when relevant. This position stand does not address acute dehydration-based weight cutting, pharmacotherapy (i.e. GLP-1RAs), or bariatric surgery. The following 15 points constitute the Position Statement of the Society; the Research Committee has approved them. 1) Diets for body weight reduction can be broadly categorized by the magnitude of the energy deficit, linearity of the deficit, and macronutrient composition. These factors need to be tailored to individual preferences, tolerances, and goals.2) Very-low-energy diets (<800 kcal/day) and low-energy diets (800-1200  kcal/day) produce greater short-term weight loss but lack long-term advantages over less aggressive energy restrictions, such as calorie-controlled diets. These aggressive diets may increase lean mass loss, although adequate protein intake and resistance training may mitigate this risk. Caution is warranted about insufficiencies in vitamins, minerals, fiber, and other nutrients.3) The evidence at-large shows a lack of differential effects between intermittent fasting variants (alternate-day fasting, time-restricted eating, and twice-weekly fasting) and continuous energy restriction on anthropometric outcomes, although macronutrient quality plays an independent role in optimizing body composition and metabolic health.4) Intra-day meal frequency (as opposed to total daily nutrition) does not tend to crucially influence body weight and body fat reduction. Meal frequency may be individualized flexibly; no lower or upper limits can universally be prescribed to optimize outcomes. However, in physically active and athletic populations, distributing protein across at least three protein-rich meals (or eating occasions) per day may optimize lean mass retention and performance during sustained energy deficits.5) Resistance training and sufficient protein intake are indispensable mitigators of lean mass loss in a sustained caloric deficit, regardless of the diet type or variant. Total daily protein is of primary importance; specific distribution of the constituent doses is a secondary concern.6) For the general population, a daily protein intake of 1.2-1.6 g/kg BW is appropriate for supporting total body weight and fat loss, physical activity, and imparting benefits to musculoskeletal and cardiometabolic health.7) Daily protein intakes ranging 1.6-2.2 g/kg BW combined with resistance training may optimize muscle anabolism, while higher intakes of 1.9-3.2 g/kg BW can maximize lean mass retention in lean, resistance-trained individuals sustaining hypocaloric conditions.8) The dietary carbohydrate‒fat proportion can be individualized to personal preference for the goal of weight loss, since the range of ketogenic to low-fat diets performs similarly.9) Ketogenic diets are effective at bodyweight and body fat reduction, but they also tend to decrease fat-free mass to a greater degree than higher-carbohydrate comparators, particularly in shorter trials where glycogen and total body water shifts can influence estimates.10) Adaptations to weight loss can be physical, physiological, and/or behavioral, and converge toward reducing energy expenditure to fulfill the body's drive toward neutralizing disruptions to homeostasis imposed by the caloric deficit.11) Adaptive thermogenesis is a reduction in resting energy expenditure beyond that predicted by changes in body composition. It can occur in response to hypocaloric conditions and weight loss, but it is not an inevitable response, and it may attenuate substantially upon attainment of weight stability.12) Metabolic adaptations that reduce energy expenditure, including adaptive thermogenesis, and impair gut microbial diversity, can often be attenuated by strategic dietary and exercise programming that foster nutrient-absorption and partitioning, and metabolic flexibility.13) A multitude of tactics can be implemented to manage and overcome plateaus. However, plateaus are also opportunities/cues to practice maintaining progress made thus far (the ultimate goal is the maintenance of a plateau).14) Guidance from an interdisciplinary team of health professionals while maintaining social support is recommended for successful weight management.15) Learning how to prepare home-cooked meals (and plan meals ahead of time through the day) puts dieters in control of their nutritional fate - and in a better position to succeed in managing their body weight and body composition.

records.title: Acute effects of 3 and 6 mg·Kg<sup>-1</sup> caffeine on strength-power performance and isokinetic peak torque in competitive male boxers: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Acute effects of 3 and 6 mg·Kg<sup>-1</sup> caffeine on strength-power performance and isokinetic peak torque in competitive male boxers: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial.
content.abstract:
Background

Evidence on the dose, timing, and task specificity of caffeine ingestion in combat-sport athletes remains limited. This study examined the acute effects of 3 and 6 mg·kg-1 caffeine on strength-power performance and isokinetic peak torque in male boxers.

Methods

Fifteen male boxers who met the Chinese national second-class athlete standard or higher completed a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial. Each participant completed placebo (PLA), 3 mg·kg-1 caffeine (CAF3), and 6 mg·kg-1 caffeine (CAF6) conditions in randomized order, separated by a 1-week washout. Countermovement jump (CMJ), ballistic push-up (BPU), and dominant-side shoulder and knee isokinetic peak torque (PT) were assessed at baseline and during testing blocks beginning at 30 and 60 min post-ingestion. Data were analyzed using two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, with Holm adjustment applied across the 10 planned condition × time interaction tests. Reliability analyzes were supportive, and threshold-based individual classifications were exploratory.

Results

Significant condition × time interactions were observed for CMJ, BPU, and isokinetic PT outcomes. During the scheduled 60-min assessment, CAF3 and CAF6 produced higher CMJ jump height, peak power, and relative peak power than PLA, with no significant difference between caffeine doses. For BPU, CAF6 produced higher concentric impulse, concentric mean power, and concentric peak power than PLA during the scheduled 60-min assessment, whereas CAF3 did not differ from PLA. Shoulder flexion and extension PT increased under caffeine conditions at selected time points, without a consistent dose advantage. Knee extension PT showed the clearest dose-specific response, with CAF6 exceeding both PLA and CAF3 during the scheduled 60-min assessment.

Conclusions

Acute ingestion of 3 and 6 mg·kg-1 caffeine was associated with improvements in selected laboratory-based strength-power and isokinetic PT outcomes in male boxers, particularly during the scheduled 60-min assessment. The pattern of responses varied across doses and testing tasks, and 6 mg·kg-1 was not consistently superior to 3 mg·kg-1. These findings should be interpreted as evidence for selected neuromuscular outcomes rather than as direct evidence of improved punching or competitive boxing performance.

records.title: Do Putative Human Reticulospinal Tract Properties Adapt Following Short-Term Isometric Resistance Training?
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Do Putative Human Reticulospinal Tract Properties Adapt Following Short-Term Isometric Resistance Training?
content.abstract:
Purpose

The primary purpose of this study was to investigate whether isometric resistance training (RT) leads to reticulospinal tract (RST) adaptations.

Methods

A "RT group" of 30 healthy adults completed 4 weeks (15 sessions) of volume-matched unilateral elbow flexion RT involving high (32 repetitions/session at 70% maximal voluntary torque [MVT]) or low (64 repetitions/session at 35%MVT) loads. An additional 15 participants served as controls (CON group). Pre- and post-test MVT, RST properties (RST gain ratio derived from the StartReact assessment; startling auditory stimulus-conditioned/control motor evoked potential [MEP] ratio; and startling stimulus-conditioned/control cervicomedullary MEP [CMEP] ratio), CST excitability and intracortical inhibition properties (in response to transcranial magnetic stimulation) were assessed.

Results

MVT increased more in the RT group (+12.8%; n = 30) vs. CON group (-4.3%; n = 15; group (2) × time (2), p = 0.001). However, changes in RST properties assessed using a series of indirect measures did not differ between the RT group (-1.4% to 6.6%; n = 30) and CON group (-4.5% to 10.5%; n = 15; group (2) × time (2), 0.352 ≤ p ≤ 0.834).

Conclusions

RST adaptations within a sample of healthy young men and women, assessed using various indirect measurement approaches, did not occur following only 4 weeks of isometric elbow flexion RT. These findings add to the currently limited scientific evidence from short-term human RT intervention studies available to inform the use of RT for healthy individuals or patients primarily targeting the development of RST function.

records.title: Beyond the Hangover: Associations Between Binge Drinking, Health, and Performance in Young Adult Resistance-Trained Females.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Beyond the Hangover: Associations Between Binge Drinking, Health, and Performance in Young Adult Resistance-Trained Females.
content.abstract:
Purpose

The present study aimed to evaluate associations between resistance training and binge drinking in relation to musculoskeletal composition, physical fitness, cognitive function, and psychological wellness in young adult females.

Methods

Participants were categorized into four groups: sedentary low alcohol consumers (SL; n=12), sedentary binge drinkers (SB; n=12), resistance-trained low alcohol consumers (RTL; n=12), and resistance-trained binge drinkers (RTB; n=12). Measurements included body composition via DEXA scan, muscle quality via ultrasonography, and insulin sensitivity via oral glucose tolerance test. Physical performance was assessed using maximum chair stand power, vertical jump, broad jump, knee extensor torque, grip strength, and push-ups to failure. Tests and questionnaires were used to assess cognitive function and psychological wellness.

Results

Resistance-trained females had lower body fat than sedentary females (RTL = 29.28±4.27%; RTB = 29.03±3.67%; SL = 37.18±5.32%; SB = 34.83±3.54%; p<0.05), and RTL had more fat-free mass than SL and SB (RTL = 48.31±5.81 kg; SL = 38.08±6.59 kg; SB = 40.37±6.05 kg; both p<0.05). There were no differences between RTL and RTB in bone mineral density, muscle quality, or physical performance. RTL outperformed SL and SB on vertical jump (both p<0.05) while RTB outperformed SL and SB on broad jump. RTL had lower fasting blood glucose than RTB (88.92±12.09 mg/dL and 103.17 ± 10.21 mg/dL, respectively; p=0.008), and lower postprandial blood glucose than all groups (RTL = 103.83±19.82 mg/dL; RTB = 137.58±21.54 mg/dL; SL = 148.50±44.60 mg/dL; SB = 139.25±14.49 mg/dL; all p<0.05).

Conclusions

The results suggest that ≥1 year of binge drinking is associated with poorer metabolic health without differences in performance in young females. Further, frequent RT may mitigate the effects of binge drinking on body composition.

records.title: Multiple Sessions of Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation Combined With Squat Training Improve Lower-Limb Maximum Strength in Healthy Adult Men.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Multiple Sessions of Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation Combined With Squat Training Improve Lower-Limb Maximum Strength in Healthy Adult Men.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Yan, X, Zuo, Z, Nitsche, MA, Zhang, X, and Qi, F. Multiple sessions of transcranial direct current stimulation combined with squat training improve lower-limb maximum strength in healthy adult men. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study aimed to investigate the effects of transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) combined with Squat training (ST) on lower-limb maximum strength in healthy adult men. Sixty men (age: 21.6 ± 2.1 years, height: 177.5 ± 5.3 cm, body mass: 73.1 ± 7.4 kg) were randomly assigned to 4 groups (tDCS + ST group, sham tDCS + ST group, tDCS + rest group, sham tDCS + rest group). The 6-week intervention program was implemented with biweekly sessions, totaling 12 treatment sessions, each separated by a minimum 48-hour interval. After the tDCS intervention, the ST groups performed squat exercises while the tDCS + rest and sham tDCS + rest groups sat quietly for 30 minutes. Lower-limb maximal muscle strength was measured at 4 distinct time points: preintervention (T0), 24 hours post-third week intervention (T1), 24 hours post-sixth week final session (T2), and 1 week post-entire intervention completion (T3). Key evaluation metrics were measured, including 1 repetition maximum (1RM) squat, knee extensor and flexor peak torque, and rectus femoris cross-sectional area (CSA). Significant improvements in 1RM, knee extensor strength, and nondominant rectus femoris CSA were observed in both tDCS + ST and sham tDCS + ST groups compared with the sham tDCS-only group (p < 0.05). No differences in knee strength, 1RM, or rectus femoris CSA were observed between the tDCS + rest and sham tDCS + rest groups. The results indicate that anodal tDCS combined with ST does not yield additional training benefits on lower-limb maximal strength in healthy adults when compared with ST alone.

records.title: Training Status and Valsalva Maneuver Effects on Cerebrovascular Regulation during Acute Resistance Exercise.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Training Status and Valsalva Maneuver Effects on Cerebrovascular Regulation during Acute Resistance Exercise.
content.abstract:
Background

Repeated exposure to large transient oscillations in mean arterial pressure (MAP)during resistance exercise may induce vascular adaptations and alter cerebrovascular regulation during systemic pressure challenges. This study characterized resting vascular and cerebrovascular function, the cerebral pressure-flow relationship during forced blood pressure oscillations, and cerebrovascular responses to leg press exercise with and without the Valsalva maneuver (VM) in resistance-trained and untrained individuals.

Hypotheses

We hypothesized that resistance-trained individuals would exhibit higher arterial stiffness and similar cerebrovascular function at rest but improved cerebrovascular regulation during systemic pressure challenges.

Methods

Forty-four healthy young adults [23 resistance-trained (12M,11F), 21 untrained (9M,12F)] completed two visits: (1) resting vascular and cerebrovascular assessment and quantification of the cerebral pressure-flow relationship via forced blood pressure oscillations; (2) assessment of systemic and cerebral hemodynamic responses during RE at 50%, 75%, and 90% 1RM. At 90% 1RM, participants performed leg press under coached breathing and VM conditions in a randomized order.

Results

No group differences were observed in resting cerebral hemodynamics, common carotid artery stiffness metrics, or cerebral pressure-flow relationship related responses. However, training effects were found for carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity (p=0.002; ηp²=0.23; untrained>trained), diastolic blood pressure (p=0.003; ηp²=0.24; untrained>trained), pulse pressure (p=0.004; ηp²=0.27; untrainedtrained). Despite higher MAPPeak in trained individuals (p=0.03; ηp²=0.19), cerebrovascular responses were similar or attenuated compared with untrained individuals. VM strain did not differ between groups, but VM use increased MAPPeak (p=0.04; ηp²=0.05) and middle cerebral artery (MCA) pulsatility index (p=0.005; ηp²=0.09), and reduced heart rate (p=0.03; ηp²=0.06).

Conclusions

Habitual resistance training and breathing strategy both influence cerebrovascular responses, potentially helping preserve cerebral perfusion during systemic pressure challenges.

records.title: Do Athletes Lose Soleus Strength Over the Course of a Season? Longitudinal Monitoring of Seated Plantar Flexion Maximum Voluntary Contraction Strength and Factors That Affect It in Australian Football Players.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Do Athletes Lose Soleus Strength Over the Course of a Season? Longitudinal Monitoring of Seated Plantar Flexion Maximum Voluntary Contraction Strength and Factors That Affect It in Australian Football Players.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Green, B, Pizzari, T, Schache, AG, Rio, EK, Evans, SCS, Cooper, S, and Murphy, MC. Do athletes lose soleus strength over the course of a season? Longitudinal monitoring of seated plantar flexion maximum voluntary contraction strength and factors that affect it in Australian football players. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The calf muscles are critical to dynamic lower-limb function in sports but are susceptible to injury. Despite its role in performance and injury, research has not evaluated soleus strength changes over the course of a season, or factors affecting it. Flexed-knee maximum plantar flexion strength was longitudinally monitored in state-league Australian footballers (2 Western Australian and 1 Victorian team) across 1-season at timepoints: preseason (T0), early in-season (T1), late in-season (T2). Generalized estimating equations evaluated strength outcomes over time (absolute, relative, asymmetry). Intrinsic factors (e.g., age, sex, injury history, sport exposure history, calf-focused resistance training) were analyzed to determine longitudinal associations with strength. Forty-one athletes (32 male, 9 female) were monitored across 210 strength measurements from T0 to T2. Absolute (T0 = 121.7 ± 27 kg; T1 = 135.2 ± 27.3 kg; T2 = 135.8 ± 25.9 kg) and relative (T0 = 1.51 ± 0.28 body mass [BM]; T1 = 1.69 ± 0.27 BM, T2 = 1.75 ± 0.26 BM) strength demonstrated longitudinal change (absolute: β = 19.33 kg, relative: β = 0.24 BM; p < 0.001). Reduced strength was associated with a recent calf injury history (relative and absolute: p < 0.001) and older age (p = 0.03). Lower strength (absolute: β = -23.53 kg, relative: β = -0.22 BM; p < 0.05) and larger asymmetry (β = 8.13 kg, p = 0.01) were detected in female athletes. Athletes can be expected to improve and maintain soleus capacity across seasonal periods. Athlete age, calf injury history, and sex can affect strength longitudinally. These findings may guide individualized prevention, performance, and postinjury benchmarking.

records.title: An Automated Blood Flow Restriction Device Is Reliable, but Not Valid, for Determining Lower Limb Occlusion Pressure in Resistance-trained Adults.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: An Automated Blood Flow Restriction Device Is Reliable, but Not Valid, for Determining Lower Limb Occlusion Pressure in Resistance-trained Adults.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Lang, D, Fallo, X, and Bennett, H. An automated blood flow restriction device is reliable, but not valid, for determining lower limb occlusion pressure in resistance-trained adults. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Blood flow restriction (BFR) exercise can improve strength, hypertrophy, and aerobic performance. Accurate limb occlusion pressure (LOP) assessment is essential for safe prescription. The AirBands is a novel automated BFR device that estimates LOP using integrated sensors, making LOP assessment easier. However, its validity and reliability are not well established in resistance-trained individuals. This study evaluated the concurrent validity of the AirBands compared with a handheld Doppler ultrasound for lower limb LOP, and its test-retest reliability, in resistance-trained adults. Twenty-six resistance-trained adults (14 males, 12 females; 24.2 ± 4.7 years) participated. For validity, LOP was measured using AirBands and Doppler in randomized order, using the same cuff. For reliability, automated LOP was measured twice, 10 minutes apart. Agreement was assessed using Bland-Altman limits of agreement and intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC). No significant difference was observed between manual (231.7 ± 17.8 mm Hg) and automated (230.8 ± 38.3 mm Hg) LOP (mean difference -0.8 mm Hg; p = 0.928), although validity ICC was poor (0.236, 95% confidence interval [CI] = -0.293 to 0.641). Bland-Altman analysis indicated proportional bias, with overestimation at lower values and underestimation at higher values. Reliability showed no significant difference between test 1 (243.0 ± 37.5 mm Hg) and test 2 (242.3 ± 40.5 mm Hg) (mean difference 1.0 mm Hg; p = 0.816) and good reliability (ICC = 0.862, 95% CI = 0.715 to 0.936). AirBands demonstrates good test-retest reliability but poor concurrent validity vs. Doppler ultrasound. Clinicians should confirm automated values using a Doppler ultrasound before prescribing BFR.

records.title: Effects of extremely low-volume high-intensity interval training combined with iron supplementation versus iron supplementation alone on postural control in young women with iron deficiency anemia: a randomized controlled trial.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Effects of extremely low-volume high-intensity interval training combined with iron supplementation versus iron supplementation alone on postural control in young women with iron deficiency anemia: a randomized controlled trial.
content.abstract:
Background

Recent research revealed postural control deterioration in young women with Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA). To address this postural deficit, it is crucial to develop intervention strategies for postural rehabilitation in these individuals. This study aimed to explore the effect of 8-week extremely low-volume high-intensity interval training (HIIT) based on plyometric exercises combined with iron supplementation versus simple iron treatment on postural control of young women with IDA.

Methods

This randomized controlled trial enrolled young women with IDA aged 18-25 years, who were randomly assigned to a training group (TG; n = 16) or a non-training group (NTG; n = 17). All participants received oral iron supplementation (ferrous sulfate, 494.5 mg/day, administered as 247.25 mg twice daily), while the TG additionally completed an 8-week extremely low-volume HIIT program based on plyometric exercises. Hemoglobin (Hb) and serum ferritin concentrations were assessed, alongside muscle endurance, reaction time performance, and postural control. Muscle endurance was evaluated using the Killy test, reaction time performance using an online simple reaction time test, and postural control using a stabilometric platform under bipodal and semi-tandem stance conditions. Postural assessments were conducted with eyes open (EO) and eyes closed (EC) on firm and foam surfaces. All outcomes were measured at baseline and 72 h after the final intervention session.

Results

After the 8-week intervention, this study demonstrated significant improvements across both groups, irrespective of the intervention. However, TG showed significantly greater post-intervention improvements than NTG in Hb concentration (P = 0.042), muscle endurance (P < 0.001), and postural control. Superior postural control in TG was observed during a bipedal stance on a foam surface (EO: P = 0.001); EC: P = 0.035), as well as during semi-tandem stance on a firm surface (EO: P = 0.015; EC: P = 0.040) and on a foam surface (EO: P = 0.019; EC: P = 0.003), compared to the NTG. With a Bonferroni-adjusted significance threshold for multiple comparisons (α = 0.00625), between-group differences in postural control remained significant for bipedal foam EO (P = 0.001) and semi-tandem foam EC (P = 0.003).

Conclusions

The study showed that women with IDA improved their postural performance regardless of the intervention used. However, an 8-week program of extremely low-volume HIIT combined with plyometric exercises and iron supplementation had a more beneficial effect compared to traditional iron therapy. These greater improvements in postural control occurred alongside greater improvements in the Hb concentration and muscle endurance in the TG compared to the NTG.

records.title: Dose-response effects of aerobic exercise on reducing depression in patients with chronic illness and comorbid depression: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Dose-response effects of aerobic exercise on reducing depression in patients with chronic illness and comorbid depression: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Importance

Aerobic exercise is an evidence-based treatment for depression. However, current exercise recommendations do not account for the limited functional capacity of patients with chronic illness and comorbid depression. Consequently, these recommendations risk being inappropriate and having low therapeutic application in this population.

Objective

To examine the dose-response relationship between aerobic exercise volume and the severity of depressive symptoms, and to determine the exercise volume needed to alleviate depressive symptoms to the minimally important difference (MID) threshold in patients with chronic illness and comorbid depression.

Data sources

We searched four databases (PubMed, Embase, Web of Science and PsycINFO) for randomised controlled trials published between database inception and May 2025, without language restrictions.

Study selection

We included studies that compared the effects of aerobic exercise interventions with passive controls on depressive symptoms in adults with chronic illness and comorbid depression.

Data extraction and synthesis

Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers using a standardised form. A random-effects meta-analysis was employed to calculate the pooled estimate (Hedges' g) and the 95% CI. Meta-regression was conducted to determine the dose-response relationship between aerobic exercise volume and the severity of depressive symptoms.

Main outcome and measure

The prespecified primary outcome was depressive symptoms and was assessed using validated depression rating scales.

Results

36 randomised controlled trials involving 2500 patients were included. Aerobic exercise compared with passive controls reduced the severity of depressive symptoms in patients with chronic illness and comorbid depression (Hedges' g: -0.73, 95% CI -0.99 to -0.46, p<0.001, I2=81%). Additionally, aerobic exercise had a dose-response effect of -0.01 (95% CI -0.016 to -0.002, p=0.014) per 10 metabolic equivalent of task minutes per week (MET-min/week) on the severity of depressive symptoms. A weekly volume of 405 MET-min/week was found to alleviate depressive symptoms to an extent perceived as important (MID) by patients with chronic illness and comorbid depression.

Conclusions and relevance

This study presents a dose-response relationship between aerobic exercise volume and the severity of depressive symptoms, suggesting that minimal volumes of aerobic exercise can confer improvements. Importantly, it informs stakeholders that achieving the WHO recommendation of 450 MET-min/week is not mandatory to elicit improvements in depressive symptoms. These findings underscore that irrespective of the functional capacity of patients with chronic illness and comorbid depression, aerobic exercise remains a viable strategy to manage their depressive symptoms.

Prospero registration number

CRD42021282103.

records.title: Combined exercise training and dietary interventions versus independent effect of exercise on ectopic fat in individuals with overweight and obesity: a systematic review, meta-analysis, and meta-regression.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Combined exercise training and dietary interventions versus independent effect of exercise on ectopic fat in individuals with overweight and obesity: a systematic review, meta-analysis, and meta-regression.
content.abstract:
Aim

While it is well established that reducing ectopic fat can help prevent insulin resistance in individuals with overweight or obesity, it remains unclear whether diet alone, exercise alone, or their combination is most effective in reducing specific ectopic fat depots. Therefore, the objective of this study was to investigate the effects of diet-only, and combined diet-plus-exercise interventions versus exercise only on ectopic fat reduction, and weight loss in adults with overweight or obesity.

Methods

Web of Science, PubMed, and Scopus were searched for original articles, published until 1 March 2024 (no limitation on publication dates) that included diet only/or exercise and diet versus exercise alone on body weight, and ectopic fat in adults with overweight or obesity. Weighted mean differences (WMD) for body weight, liver fat, standardized mean differences (SMD) for visceral fat area (VFA), and intramuscular triglyceride (IMTG), and 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) were determined using random-effects models. Studies using noninvasive imaging techniques such as Computerized Tomography (CT), Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), and hydrogen-based Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy (H-MRs) for ectopic fat were included in this meta-analysis.

Results
